Key points
To explain:
• How the various forms of vitamin B6 in the diet are converted to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) in our organs and tissues
• How PLP acts as a cofactor for numerous enzymes, particularly those involving amino acids
• How dietary constituents and drugs that bind PLP can increase the amount of B6 an individual needs to avoid symptoms of
PLP deﬁciency
• How inborn errors of metabolism can have a similar effect.

To show how dietary deﬁciency of B6 and the effects of drugs and inborn errors of metabolism have taught us that:
• The principal effects of PLP deﬁciency are neurological including seizures, movement disorder and polyneuropathy
• Deﬁciency can, however, also cause other disorders such as anemia
• These effects can be traced to reduced activity of PLP-dependent enzymes
